description: We're experienced software engineers with a space background and product thinking interested in Mars, technology and advancing the frontier.
summary: Mars Traverse is a map that helps an astronaut plan a safe walk on Mars and do science on the way. It runs in any web browser. You pick a start, a destination, and stops. The app plans the fastest safe route on NASA terrain models of 1 m resolution and gives one ruling: GO, GO WITH CAUTION, or NO GO. The ruling covers life support, carried load, daylight, shadow, radio contact, dust, space weather, radiation, slope, loose ground, and obstacles. Along the route, the app lists the geologic units, the minerals that orbiters detect, and the rock chemistry that the rovers measured. It shows rover Navcam views at each stop so the crew knows what to expect. A 3D preview lets the crew walk the route first on real terrain, with a helmet display. The map combines eight kinds of data from more than ten NASA missions. This is important because the first crews will have hours, not days, of life support on each walk and every step will be the first ever taken. They must know before they leave whether a walk is safe and what they will find along the way.
details:
What it does

Mars Traverse answers the three needs of the challenge: the route and its destinations, the current conditions, and the science along the way.

Route and destinations. The planner finds the fastest route for five kinds of traveller: an astronaut on foot, an open crewed rover, a pressurized rover, an autonomous rover, and a hopper. A climb costs time. If a detour around a hill is faster, the route goes around the hill. You can add up to 8 stops, each with a stay time. A walk with stops is a loop that comes back to the start. The panel gives the distance, the time, the climb, the life support used, and the point of no return. The route avoids slopes above the limit of the traveller, loose sand (from THEMIS thermal inertia), and obstacles. At six HiRISE sites, the build finds obstacles from their shadows in the orbital image: boulders, small craters, and steep edges. An obstacle with more relief than the traveller can cross blocks the way.

Safety. The planner models a crew of two, as NASA plans its EVAs. Carried equipment slows the walkers, from the Pandolf load carriage equation that NASA uses for EVA planning. Life support keeps a 25% reserve. For a start time, the app marks the parts of the route in terrain shadow or after dark. It also marks the parts with no radio line of sight to the habitat. It lists the relay orbiter passes during the walk. It gives the radiation dose from Curiosity RAD, over the solar cycle, against the NASA career limit. A coronal mass ejection from NASA DONKI that reaches Mars near the walk turns the check to NO GO.

Current conditions. For any place and season, the app gives the local solar time, sunrise, and sunset. It gives the normal dust and the dust storm risk over 13 Mars years. It also gives the model climate from the NASA Ames Mars GCM, the newest weather from Perseverance MEDA and Curiosity REMS, and the space weather. A habitat display mode shows the status of a base now in large text: the time, the sun, EVA alerts, the window for a full EVA today, and the next relay passes.

Science along the way. The app lists the geologic units that a route crosses, from USGS maps. In Jezero and on Mount Sharp, it gives the minerals that MRO CRISM detects near the route. It lists about 6,400 rock and soil measurements from Curiosity (APXS and ChemCam) and Perseverance (PIXL), with notable values highlighted. It suggests stops at unit contacts and near minerals. A ready-made excursion goes to the boxwork on Mount Sharp, the example of the challenge. At each stop, it shows the Navcam images from the nearest rover stop, so the crew knows what to expect.

Beyond the rover sites. Crews will land where there is water ice, not where the rovers are. So the app has ten more sites with HiRISE terrain models of 1 m. Two are SpaceX Starship candidate sites. Others are two scarps of exposed ice, an ice-rich debris apron, the ExoMars and InSight landing sites, and three NASA candidate Exploration Zones. The SWIM subsurface ice map gives the ice values at each site. Each site has a ready-made walk.

3D preview. The preview builds the ground around the route from the HiRISE and CTX terrain and images. The sun stands where it will at the chosen time. The traveller walks the route, and a helmet heads-up display shows the heading, the next stop, life support, dose, and the time to sunset. The preview also works in a VR headset. Some detail is generated, such as small rocks and the texture below 25 cm, and the preview says so on screen. A cue card exports each walk as a printable page with the steps, stops, limits, and warnings.

How it works

The app has no server of its own that it depends on. The data build (Python with rasterio, numpy, and scipy) downloads NASA products from the Planetary Data System, USGS, and Mars Trek. It converts them to map tiles and small vector files, and uploads them to Cloudflare R2 as static files. The static browser app (React, CesiumJS, and Three.js) reads those files. The route planner, the orbit model, the sun model, and all the checks run in the browser. On Mars they must run on the device, because Earth servers are minutes away. A small Cloudflare Worker serves the app and runs an hourly job. The job reads the rover positions, the weather, the space weather, and new orbit elements from NASA services.

Benefits

The crew sees in one place whether a walk is safe and how long it takes. The same view gives the cost in life support and dose, and the science on the way. The planning works offline once the data is loaded. The same app works on a tablet in the habitat, on a wall display, and in a headset.

What we hope to achieve

We want to show that the open data of NASA missions already gives most of what a crew needs to plan a Marswalk. With rock maps from new orbital images and live weather from more landers, the same app can support the first crewed missions and also serve as a real time display for active walks with multiple tracked elements.

How it is creative

- No rock map exists for most of Mars. So the build measures the shadows in HiRISE images to find boulders, small craters, and steep edges, and the route goes around them.

- Rover Navcam images become a street view for astronauts. At each stop, the app shows the images from the nearest rover stop, and the view toward the direction of travel comes first.

- All the planning runs in the browser, on static files. A crew on Mars cannot wait for a server on Earth.

- Many checks give one ruling. The crew reads GO, GO WITH CAUTION, or NO GO first, and each check is one tap away.

- The same plan works on three displays: a tablet, a habitat wall, and a helmet display in a 3D preview or a VR headset.

- The sites go beyond the rovers. Ten more sites include candidate landing sites, places with water ice, and NASA candidate Exploration Zones.

What we considered

- Safety first. Life support keeps a 25% reserve, astronauts walk in pairs, and the map marks the point of no return. Each limit comes from a NASA document, or the app marks it as an assumption.

- Data providence. The app marks each estimate and each generated detail in order to go to the source of the data as needed.

- Tests against real data. We compared the route planner with 66 real drives of Perseverance and Curiosity. The planner found a route for every one. The planned routes are 10% to 18% shorter than the real drives at the median, so a planned distance is a lower limit.

- The delay to Earth. The app needs no server for its planning, and it works offline once the data is loaded.

- Small screens. The panels fit a phone, and the habitat display uses large text.

Tools Used

JavaScript, React, CesiumJS, Three.js, Vite, and Vitest for the browser app. Cloudflare Workers, Durable Objects, and R2 for hosting. Python, rasterio (GDAL), numpy, scipy, Pillow, pyogrio, and httpx for the data build. Claude, an AI coding assistant, helped write the code (see "Use of Super Intelligence").
